Routing notes:
- All examples involve large requests from the east region; region alone does not determine the answer.
- “C” was accepted for a shipment explicitly noted as coming through the regional office. Treat regional-office wording as strong evidence for the regional-office option when available.
- Repeated follow-up wording (“asking about this twice already”) was successfully routed to B (priority desk) for both invoice and refund requests.
- Do not assume B for every retry/follow-up: “Second attempt, the first form bounced,” “Let me know if anything is missing,” and “No rush” were all rejected when routed to B.
- A refund described as “same as the ones I sent last month” was rejected when routed to C; this wording does not indicate the regional-office route.
- “Same as the ones I sent last month” led to an accepted D for an invoice, but the evidence is too sparse to generalize.
- “Paperwork was scanned, not typed” led to rejection for a claim at D, while the same wording led to acceptance for an invoice at B; request type matters.
- Do not infer a universal mapping from sender department or person; examples across Client Services, Finance, Partner Accounts, Regional Ops, and Field Sales vary.
- Verify the complete option text before choosing: some records truncate option labels and include apparently inconsistent fourth options.

Routing notes:
- All examples involve large east-region requests; region, sender department/person, and request type can affect routing, but none alone determines the answer.
- Verify the complete option text before choosing. Truncated labels and apparently inconsistent fourth options are common; an option may be invalid even when its visible label appears to match prior guidance.
- “C” is not reliably indicated by “came in through the regional office”: this wording led to C being rejected for both renewal and invoice requests. Treat it as a clue only, not a rule.
- “Our client has been asking about this twice already” led to accepted B for an invoice; earlier evidence also supports B for a refund. Repeated follow-up may indicate B, but do not generalize without request context.
- “Second attempt, the first form bounced” was not B in prior examples and was rejected when tried as A for an invoice and D for a refund. It remains unresolved, not a reliable mapping.
- “Let me know if anything is missing” was rejected as A for a claim; “No rush, but please confirm receipt” was accepted as A for a renewal.
- “Hoping this can go out before end of day” was accepted as A for both a transfer and a refund.
- “Paperwork was scanned, not typed” was accepted as A for a refund, but rejected as D for a claim and accepted as B for an invoice; request type clearly matters.
- “Same as the ones I sent last month” was rejected as C for a refund and accepted as D for an invoice; evidence is too sparse to generalize.

Routing notes:
- All examples involve large east-region requests. Region, sender department/person, request type, wording, and the complete option list may affect routing; no single factor determines the answer.
- Always verify the complete option text. Truncated labels and missing/invalid fourth options are frequent. Do not select an option whose label is absent or incomplete, even if prior guidance suggests it.
- “Came in through the regional office” was rejected as C for renewal and invoice; treat it only as a clue.
- “No rush, but please confirm receipt” was accepted as A for a renewal; “Hoping this can go out before end of day” was accepted as A for both transfer and refund.
- “Our client has been asking about this twice already” is context-dependent: B was accepted for invoice, but rejected for renewal, refund, and two shipment examples. One shipment with this wording accepted A. Do not generalize.
- “Let me know if anything is missing” is unresolved and request-dependent: A was rejected for claim, refund, and one shipment; D was invalid for another shipment.
- “Second attempt, the first form bounced” remains unresolved; prior A, B, and D trials were rejected in different contexts.
- “Paperwork was scanned, not typed” varies by request: A accepted for refund, B accepted for invoice, D rejected for claim.
- “Same as the ones I sent last month” remains unresolved: C and D were rejected for refunds (D was invalid).
- Sender department/person may matter, but current evidence is too sparse for reliable sender-based rules.
